analysis.one_liner: Forces people to give businesses months of notice before suing over entrances blocked to disabled customers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee after one June 2012 hearing and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, a person who cannot get into a store because of a physical barrier, like stairs and no ramp, can sue the owner directly. This bill would have changed that: the person would first have to send written notice identifying the barrier, wait 60 days for the owner to describe planned fixes, and then wait up to 120 more days for the work to be finished before going to court. Supporters framed it as protection for business owners from surprise lawsuits; disability advocates have long argued such notice-and-cure requirements let inaccessible businesses delay fixing their entrances.
analysis.who_benefits: Business and property owners whose buildings have structural barriers to entry. If sued under the ADA today, they face a lawsuit immediately. Under this bill, a disabled customer would have to give written notice, then wait 60 days for the owner to reply with a plan, then up to 120 more days for the barrier to actually be removed — roughly six months total — before court was an option.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of buildings with blocked entrances

how_it_helps.text: Requires a disabled person to send the owner a written notice specific enough to identify the barrier before any lawsuit can be filed.
Gives the owner 60 days after notice to provide a written description of the improvements they will make to remove the barrier.
Gives the owner up to 120 more days after providing that description to actually remove the barrier before a suit could begin.

analysis.who_pays: Disabled customers who are kept out of stores, restaurants, and other public accommodations. They would have to wait months before they could take a business to court, and a business could promise fixes and let the clock run.

drawbacks.text: A person denied access because of a structural barrier could not sue for up to roughly 180 days — 60 days for a response plus 120 days for promised fixes — meaning months of being kept out of a business with no legal recourse.

A business could satisfy the notice requirement by sending a written description of improvements it has no obligation to complete on time, and only then would the 120-day removal clock start — allowing repeated delay without penalty.

Disability rights advocates have long argued that private lawsuits are a main way the ADA's entry requirements get enforced at all, so adding a cure period weakens the law's practical force for the people it was written to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Business owners do face real costs from ADA barrier suits, and a notice-and-cure period gives a good-faith owner a chance to fix a problem without litigation. But the cost of this design lands on disabled customers: months of continued exclusion, and an owner could buy time by describing fixes without finishing them. The bill gave businesses a shield before giving disabled people any guarantee of access, which is why disability advocates opposed this type of requirement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Constitution subcommittee, got a single hearing in June 2012, and then sat until the Congress ended without ever reaching a committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lungren introduced the bill on November 3, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 21, 2011, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution.
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 27, 2012, but no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with 17 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Disabled people kept the current rule that they can sue a business over a blocked entrance without waiting months, and business owners gained nothing. Because the bill never became law, the people it would have shielded — owners of inaccessible buildings — did not get the notice-and-cure protection it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Disabled customers keeping current lawsuit rights

for.name: Rep. Daniel E. Lungren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring notice and a compliance period before ADA barrier lawsuits.

for.name: 17 of 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

for.name: Business and property-owner groups
for.what_they_did: Longstanding supporters of notification bills like this one, which shield owners of older buildings from immediate ADA suits.

against.name: Lamar Smith
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote; after a June 2012 subcommittee hearing, no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

against.name: Disability rights advocates
against.what_they_did: Have opposed notice-and-cure requirements for ADA access suits, arguing they let inaccessible businesses delay removing barriers that keep disabled customers out.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Republicans with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill stalled in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee after one hearing.

industries.industry: Retail stores, restaurants, and small businesses in older buildings
industries.note: The bill would have given owners of buildings with blocked entrances up to about six months of lawsuit protection after notice, without guaranteeing the barrier gets removed. Their gain — fewer or delayed suits — comes at the cost of disabled customers staying locked out longer.
Owners would get a 60-day response window and a 120-day cure window before any tenant's or customer's ADA suit could proceed, shifting leverage toward property owners.

industries.industry: Law firms handling ADA accessibility suits
industries.note: A mandatory notice-and-cure period would cut demand for barrier-removal suits. Some of this litigation is abusive, but private suits are also one of the main ways the ADA's entry rules get enforced.
